name: Part 2 — Long Turn
tagline: One minute to plan, two minutes alone with the examiner listening
blurb: The long turn is the only part of the test where nobody rescues you. It is also the easiest part to prepare for, because the cue cards are finite in type and a well-built story adapts across many of them.

facts: Exactly one minute, with paper and a pencil provided. You may write anything you like.
One to two minutes. The examiner starts a timer.
At two minutes the examiner will stop you. This is the outcome to aim for, not a failure.
A topic plus three or four prompts, and a final and explain… which is the one that carries most of the development.
One or two short questions afterwards. These are not part of the long turn but they are assessed, and they are where memorised answers tend to collapse.
brief.what: The descriptors for this part turn on two phrases. Band 7 requires that you speak at length without noticeable effort; Band 8 requires that you develop topics coherently and appropriately. Note what is absent from both: any requirement to cover every prompt, and any requirement for the content to be true. The prompts are scaffolding for candidates who would otherwise run dry. If you have a better structure, the scaffolding is optional.
myths: “I must cover all four bullet points.”
There are no marks attached to the bullets. There are marks attached to running out of material at ninety seconds, which is what the bullets exist to prevent.

Examiners are trained to detect memorisation, and the rounding-off question is designed to expose it. A memorised answer that unravels under one follow-up question costs more than an imperfect spontaneous one.
“I should write full sentences in the minute.”
Sentences get read aloud, and reading aloud is instantly audible. Notes should be nouns.
“Stopping early is fine if I've said everything.”
Under Fluency and Coherence, an answer that ends at fifty seconds has not demonstrated the ability to speak at length. It caps the band regardless of accuracy.

tactics.name: The sixty-second note
tactics.why: What you write in the preparation minute determines whether you narrate or recite.
tactics.do: Five to seven nouns down the left margin, plus two verbs. Nouns are retrieval cues; they cannot be read aloud. For a cue card about a difficult decision: transfer form · Tết dinner · cousin's weekend · eight months · outsource.
tactics.dont: Full sentences, or a copy of the four bullets. Copying the bullets produces a list.

band.b7: Notes are cues, not sentences, and include one vivid detail.
band.b8: Notes include the closing line, written first. Knowing where you land lets you pace everything before it.

tactics.name: Open in the middle of the action
tactics.why: I would like to talk about… announces preparation and spends five seconds saying nothing. The first sentence is where the examiner decides whether this is a person talking or a person reciting.
tactics.do: Start with the event, a time stamp, or a contradiction. Two years ago I did something my family still hasn't quite forgiven me for.
tactics.dont: Today I am going to describe a difficult decision that I made in my life.

band.b6: Opens with a clear statement of the topic.
band.b7: Opens with a specific moment or detail rather than a label.
band.b8: Opens with two short opposed clauses that set a rhythm — The decision took forty seconds. Living with it took two years.

tactics.name: The tense spine
tactics.why: Grammatical Range in Part 2 is won almost entirely on narrative tenses, and they arrive naturally only if you know which does what.
tactics.do: Past simple carries the events. Past continuous sets the scene behind them. Past perfect handles anything that happened earlier. I was revising for finals when the message came through. I had been waiting three weeks for it.
tactics.dont: Past simple for everything, which flattens the story and caps Grammatical Range at Band 6.

band.b7: Past simple with past continuous and at least one past perfect.
band.b8: Tense shifts used for effect — a switch to present for the vivid moment, then back.

tactics.name: One line of direct speech
tactics.why: This is the cheapest high-yield device available. Quoting somebody forces a change of voice, pitch and pace, which is exactly the flexible intonation the Band 8 pronunciation descriptor asks for.
tactics.do: He said, “Sit with the boring part for two days and see if you're still curious.”
tactics.dont: Reported speech throughout, which keeps the delivery monotone.

band.b8: Quotes a line containing a self-correction, which forces a mid-utterance intonation shift.

tactics.name: Bank a reflection ending
tactics.why: Running out of material at ninety seconds is the commonest Part 2 failure, and a prepared closing move solves it permanently.
tactics.do: Keep three portable endings that fit any cue card: What stayed with me was… / With hindsight… / I still think about it whenever… Each buys twenty to thirty seconds of genuine development.
tactics.dont: So that is the story I wanted to tell. Thank you. This forfeits the ending and signals rehearsal.

band.b8: Closes on an observation that outlives the anecdote and was not obvious from the opening.

tactics.name: The stretch kit
tactics.why: When the examiner has not stopped you and you have said everything, you need three reliable ways to add twenty seconds without padding.
tactics.do: Sensory detail — what the place smelled or sounded like. Contrast with now — how you would handle it today. A second person's reaction — what somebody else said or did about it.
tactics.dont: Repeating the same point in different words, which the descriptors name explicitly as repetition.

band.b7: Adds one of the three moves above.
band.b8: Adds the move that most advances the point, not the first one to hand.

tactics.name: One story, many cards
tactics.why: There are sixty-six cue cards in the forecast and perhaps eight underlying story shapes. Preparing sixty-six stories is neither possible nor useful.
tactics.do: Build four story stems and learn to re-angle them. A single story about switching university course serves a difficult decision, a change you made, a time you changed an opinion, an important decision, a person who influenced you and an ambition. Change the first and last thirty seconds; the middle stays.
tactics.dont: Telling the identical story regardless of the card, which examiners hear as off-topic and which costs coherence marks.

band.b6: Has a story ready for the common types.
band.b7: Re-angles the opening and closing to the card asked.
band.b8: Re-angles the emphasis throughout so the same events genuinely answer a different question.

lang.intro: Part 2 language is narrative language. Four functions carry almost every long turn: sequencing time, setting a scene, reporting reaction, and reflecting at the close.

items: Compresses two events into one clause. By the time I got there, it had already started.
Instant sequence, more vivid than when. The moment I saw her face I knew.
Inversion, and therefore high-value grammar. Use once. No sooner had we sat down than the power went out.
In the end is the outcome; at the end is a position in time. Candidates confuse these constantly.
Delays a reveal, which is how you build tension. It wasn't until the following week that I understood why.
Invites recognition without description. It was one of those afternoons where nothing quite works.
Direct address to the listener. Used sparingly it is striking; twice it is a mannerism.
you could hear a pin drop
Complete silence. Reserve for a genuinely tense moment.
Hidden and hard to find, with positive connotation. A tiny café tucked away behind the market.
Understated astonishment, which lands better in English than an emphatic version.
One syllable, maximum effect. Short sentences at the crisis point are a pacing device as much as a lexical one.
Judging with knowledge you did not have at the time. Almost always fronted.
Introduces the lasting impression. A reliable closing frame.
Direct and slightly plain — upgrade to what I took from it was.
Common and safe; vary it with in retrospect for a more formal register.
I'd be lying if I said
Admits a cost honestly. A narrative with no cost in it sounds invented.

phon.intro: Two minutes of continuous speech is enough time for rhythm to become the dominant impression. These three features are what turn an accurate long turn into a fluent one.

items.what: Speech is delivered in thought groups of roughly four to seven words, with a brief pause between them. A pause at a thought boundary reads as planning; a pause in the middle of a phrase reads as searching for a word. The descriptors treat these very differently: hesitation to prepare content is a Band 9 feature, hesitation to find language is not.
items.drill: The deCIsion itself / took about FORty seconds ↘ ‖ (silence, half a second) ‖ LIVing with it / took TWO years ↘
items.note: Do not fill the pause with um. Filled pauses are heard as hesitation; silent ones are heard as control. This is the single highest-value pronunciation habit in Part 2.

items.what: A story told at one speed flattens. Crisis points want short clauses delivered quickly; reflection wants longer clauses delivered slowly.
items.drill: Fast and clipped: I froze. The screen went black. Nothing. ‖ Slow and extended: What stayed with me, more than the panic itself, was how calmly everybody around me carried on.
items.note: Record both halves and check that the second is audibly slower. Most candidates produce no difference at all on the first attempt.

items.what: When you quote somebody, English speakers shift pitch and often pace. Delivering a quotation in your own narrative voice wastes the device entirely.
items.drill: He said — (lower, slower) “SPEND a weekend on the TEdious part. NOT the exciting part — the TEdious part.”
items.note: The self-correction inside the quotation forces a mid-utterance intonation shift, which is precisely what the Band 8 descriptor means by using intonation flexibly.

drills.name: Full simulation
drills.set: One cue card, sixty seconds of notes, then speak until stopped at two minutes.
drills.aim: The only drill that tests the real thing. Do it at least twice a week. Check the recording ends because the timer ended, not because you did.

drills.name: Ninety-second floor
drills.set: One cue card, no preparation at all, minimum ninety seconds.
drills.aim: Builds the stretch kit. When you feel yourself running dry, reach for sensory detail, contrast with now, or a second person's reaction.

drills.name: Same story, four cards
drills.set: One story stem told four times against four different cue cards.
drills.aim: Trains re-angling. The middle should stay constant while the first and last thirty seconds change completely.

drills.name: Rounding-off survival
drills.set: One cue card, then answer two follow-up questions immediately with no pause.
drills.aim: Memorised answers fail here. If the follow-up feels hard, the long turn was recited rather than told.

check: fc
The recording ran to at least ninety seconds and I did not stop before the timer.
fc
I opened with a specific moment rather than an announcement of the topic.
fc
Pauses fell at thought boundaries rather than inside phrases.
fc
The turn had a shape — opening, complication, resolution, reflection — not a list of four prompts.
lr
There was at least one vivid concrete detail nobody could have memorised for me.
lr
I closed on a reflection rather than on that is my story.
gr
The narrative used past continuous for background and at least one past perfect.
gr
Sentence length varied with the moment — short at the crisis, long at the reflection.
pr
At least one line of direct speech was delivered in a changed voice.
pr
There was at least one deliberate silent pause, unfilled.

strategies.intro: Every cue card in the forecast belongs to one of six families, and each family has a shape that reliably fills two minutes. Learning six shapes is a far better investment than preparing sixty-six answers — and it is what lets one prepared story serve five or six different cards.

groups.cue: Twenty-one of the sixty-six Q3 cue cards. The largest family by some distance.
groups.shape: Identity → Relationship → One defining scene → What they changed in you
moves: Spend no more than fifteen seconds on who they are. Candidates routinely spend a minute on biography and run out of time before saying anything interesting.
The defining scene is the whole answer. One occasion, narrated properly, with what they said.
Close on effect, not on adjectives. She is very kind is Band 6. I still hear her voice when I want to give up is not.
Physical description is almost always wasted time. Nobody is marking you on appearance.

ex.q: Describe a person you know who is very organised
ex.a: Open on a scene — the shared spreadsheet that appeared in the group chat forty minutes after the project was assigned — then work outwards to who she is and what that habit does to everyone around her.

groups.trap: A list of admirable qualities. Four adjectives with no scene behind them reads as a character reference, not a description.

groups.cue: Twelve cards in the Q3 set, including quiet, noisy, crowded, boring, natural and recommended places.
groups.shape: Locate in one line → Two senses → What you do there → Why it persists in memory
moves: Locate it quickly and move on. Directions are not description.
Two senses, not five. Sound and smell do more than sight because candidates never use them.
The middle section should be an activity, not a survey. What you do there is more interesting than what is there.
For negative cards — boring, noisy — the reason must be specific to that place, not a general complaint about noise.

ex.q: Describe a quiet place that you would love to go to
ex.a: The reading room smells of dust and floor polish, and the loudest sound is the radiator. Then: what you would do there, who you would take, and why quiet has become something you have to go looking for.

groups.trap: Turning it into a travel brochure. Adjectives such as beautiful, amazing and peaceful carry no lexical weight because everyone uses them.

groups.cue: Gifts, purchases, technology, cakes, traditional products.
groups.shape: What it is → How it came to you → How you actually use it → What it says about you
moves: The acquisition story is where the narrative tenses live. Use it.
Describe use, not specification. Nobody is marking the product; they are marking your relationship to it.
The final move — what it reveals about you — is what separates this from a catalogue entry.
One physical detail is enough, and it should be an odd one: a scratch, a smell, a fault you have never fixed.

ex.q: Describe a gift you would like to buy for your friend
ex.a: Since the card is hypothetical, the tense spine is conditional: I'd probably go for…, because she'd never buy it herself, and she'd pretend not to like it for about a week.

groups.trap: Listing features. A specification is not a description, and it produces no grammar beyond the present simple.

groups.cue: The narrative family: decisions, problems, journeys, parties, waiting, things going wrong.
moves: This is the only family where a true story clearly outperforms an invented one, because the details come free.
The complication must arrive within thirty seconds. A story where nothing goes wrong has no second minute.
Reaction is where the emotional vocabulary belongs — my heart sank, I was completely thrown.
Resolution can be partial or negative. A story that fails is often better material than one that succeeds.

ex.q: Describe a time when you were stuck in a traffic jam for a very long time
ex.a: Setting in two lines, then the complication — the moment the radio said the bridge was closed — then what you did for three hours, then what it changed about how you travel now.

groups.trap: Telling the events in the order they happened with no shape. Chronology is not structure.

groups.cue: Habits, routines, hobbies, sports, things you regret doing.
groups.shape: What → How it started → What it looks like in practice → Why it persists
moves: The origin story gives you the past tenses that a pure habit description cannot.
Describe one typical instance in the present tense rather than summarising all instances.
Why it persists is a better closing question than why I like it, because it forces something more honest.
For negative cards — a waste of time — be specific about what the time could have bought instead.

ex.q: Describe an activity you do regularly that you think is a waste of time
ex.a: Forty minutes every evening scrolling through videos I will not remember tomorrow. Then: when it started, what a typical evening actually looks like, and why knowing it is a waste has changed nothing.

groups.trap: Explaining the benefits of the activity in general. Health benefits of exercise are not a description of your exercise.

groups.type: MEDIA & ABSTRACT — Describe an advertisement / law / piece of news / video
groups.cue: The family candidates handle worst, because there is no story to fall back on.
groups.shape: Content in thirty seconds → Your encounter with it → Your reaction → Why it matters beyond you
moves: Summarise the content fast and stop. A two-minute plot summary is the standard failure here.
Your encounter — where you were, why you were watching — supplies the narrative the card lacks.
Reaction must be specific. I found it interesting is the weakest sentence available in Part 2.
The closing move is the Part 3 move brought forward: why this matters to people other than you.

ex.q: Describe an advertisement with a famous person in it
ex.a: Thirty seconds on what happens in the advert, then where you were when you first saw it and why it stopped you, then what it was really selling, which is never the product.

groups.trap: Describing the thing and never appearing in the answer yourself. The card says describe, but the marks are in your relationship to it.

extra.title: One story, five cards — the re-angling table
extra.html:
Sixty-six cue cards, six families, and perhaps eight underlying stories. The work is not writing sixty-six answers; it is learning to re-angle four or five stories so that they genuinely answer different questions.

A single story — switching university course against family expectation — legitimately serves all of these from the Q3 forecast:

Cue cardWhat changes
A time you changed an important decisionOpen on the reversal; the family conflict is background.
A change that you made recentlyOpen on life before and after; the decision itself is one line.
A time you changed an important opinionForeground what you believed about safe careers and why it broke.
A person you know who did something difficultRe-centre on the cousin who refused to advise you. You become the witness.
A long-term goal you would like to achieveUse the story as the origin of the goal; spend the second minute forward, not back.

The rule. The first thirty seconds and the last thirty seconds change completely. The middle minute stays. If the opening does not use the exact language of the card, the examiner hears an off-topic answer — and off-topic costs more than any lexical gain the prepared story delivers.

Build four stems, not eight. One about a decision, one about a failure, one about a person who changed something, one about a place that matters. Between them they reach roughly forty of the sixty-six cards in this quarter's forecast.
